summary: The note surveys how regional fishing calendars shape local seafood dishes across the seasons, from autumn oysters to winter Skrei and summer lobster and salmon. It then examines how overfishing and climate change are shifting migrations and forcing chefs to adapt. It closes on aquaculture as a possible solution and the uncertain cultural future of wild catch seasons.
one_line: Regional seafood seasons and dishes are being reshaped by overfishing and climate change, pushing chefs toward new species and aquaculture.
key_facts: Dr. Emily Richardson of the New England Marine Conservation Institute says oysters are prime in colder months due to slower metabolisms and lower chances of bacteria flourishing.
Louisiana shrimper James Fontenot prepares for white shrimp season, which peaks as summer heat yields to milder temperatures.
The Sicilian 'mattanza', a ritualistic tuna catch, culminates in late spring, and the tuna is cured and preserved for year-round consumption.
Skrei, migratory cod traveling from the Barents Sea to spawn along the Norwegian coast, is eaten from February to April, according to Oslo chef Ingrid Solvik.
Dungeness crab is a winter treat celebrated in the Pacific Northwest.
Sakura Masu, or cherry salmon, makes a seasonal run around the Japanese archipelago in spring.
Maine lobsterman Pete Connors marks late June, when lobsters molt and produce soft-shell 'shedder' lobsters.
Summer brings a surge of blue crabs in the Chesapeake Bay and the start of the wild salmon season in Alaska.
Overfishing has led to the collapse of some stocks, such as the Atlantic cod.
Squid normally found in southern waters are being sighted more frequently in the North because of warmer ocean temperatures, per UK fisherman Richard Thomson.
Chef Luisa Santos of coastal Portugal is experimenting with mackerel and other more sustainable options for dishes like Bacalhau à Brás and sardines on toast.
Chef Takumi Hashimoto of Hakodate is reviving old recipes that use overlooked local fish varieties.
The FAO estimates that over one-third of fish stocks are harvested at biologically unsustainable levels.
Jenna McLeod leads research into sustainable fish farming techniques at Oceana and argues aquaculture done right can relieve wild stocks.
